title: The bowl upstream
hookLine: a later telling: he sets the bowl on the river; if it floats upstream he will awaken, and it does
last: PAYASA — FEED THE ONE WHO WALKS.

cards: If the light turns green before I get there, it's a sign. If the next song is our song, I'll call. People make small bargains like these with the world when something big is on their minds, half joking, half hoping.
The wanderer has eaten Sujata's milk-rice and bathed in the river Neranjara. The telling says he's holding the empty golden bowl, standing at the water's edge. Tonight, he senses, is the night.
And he makes a bargain of his own, except the stakes are everything.

teach.b: This comes from the later telling, not the suttas. He sets the bowl on the river and says: if I'm going to become a Buddha today, let this bowl float upstream. If not, let it go with the current.
And the bowl turns, and floats against the flow of the river, straight upstream, a long way, the story says, and then sinks.
It sinks down to the palace of a serpent king under the river, and lands with a little click against three other bowls: the bowls of three Buddhas who came before. Why this image?
A river is a plain picture of the way things usually go. Downstream. Gravity.
Habit. And in a sutta, the Buddha describes what he found as going against the stream: subtle, deep, hard to see for people who delight in clinging.
Someone who has entered the path is called a sotapanna, a stream-enterer, which pictures the path itself as a river running toward freedom.
So the bowl floating upstream can be read as the teaching in one picture: what he's about to find moves against the flow of wanting.
Look back at this week: five companions, the breath held till his head roared, dukkarakarika, six years, jambu, Sujata's bowl, and now this one.
Again and again, the hard way failed, and something gentler pointed forward.

how: The bowl floating upstream appears in Buddhist temple murals, including in Thailand, and teachers use it to picture the dharma as going against the stream of craving.

the village near Uruvela where Sujata lived

games.q: you set the golden bowl on the river: if you'll awaken today, let it float upstream. what happens?
o: it sinks right where you set it.
it floats upstream, against the current.
games.why: in the telling, it floats upstream a long way, then sinks, clicking against the bowls of three earlier Buddhas.

practice: Bring to mind one hope you've been holding tightly, a result, a reply, a change, and picture setting it on a river, the way the wanderer set down his bowl.

You're not giving up on it, just not clutching it anymore; watch it float, since where it goes is not entirely up to you. Feel your hands, empty now, resting in your lap, and let the breath come and go.

wordCard.voice: Neranjara. The river where, in the later telling, the wanderer set his golden bowl, which floated upstream against the current as a sign he would awaken.

orig.note: Pali: the river Neranjara, near Uruvela, where the Buddha bathed on the day of his awakening.

carryVoice: Your line: against the current. The week of the ascetics ends here. Seven weeks, done.
